Chapter 3: The Trap of Straight-Line Thinking and the Complexity of Change.
Have you ever caught yourself thinking, "If things keep going the way they are, we’ll be in big trouble"? It’s a really common mistake, and it happens because we tend to believe that today’s trends will just keep going in a straight line—no twists, no turns. Let’s say a city’s population is booming. It’s easy to imagine that if this keeps up, it’ll double or even triple in no time. Suddenly, everyone’s worried about overcrowding and running out of resources. But here’s the thing: most trends don’t actually move in a straight, unbroken path.
Real change? It’s messy. It’s shaped by feedback loops, limits, and those moments where everything shifts. Take population growth. As societies become wealthier and healthier, something interesting happens—families usually have fewer children. When kids are more likely to survive, and women have better access to education and jobs, birth rates drop. That’s why global population growth is already slowing down, and experts predict it’ll actually level off later this century. And it’s not just population. You can see the same pattern in economic growth, how quickly we adopt new technologies, even how our environment changes. At first, things might take off really fast. But eventually, other factors kick in, and the pace slows or even levels out. So, how do you avoid falling into the straight-line trap? Here are a few things you can try:
Ask yourself—what could change the trend? What might slow it down, stop it, or even turn it around? Look for moments in the past where things didn’t just keep going up or down, but instead bent or plateaued. Think bigger than just one piece of data—look at the whole system.
For example, when people worry about overpopulation, they often miss the fact that birth rates fall as living standards improve. And when it comes to running out of resources, we sometimes forget about the ways technology helps us do more with less, or find totally new solutions.
The real takeaway? Most trends aren’t linear. Once you see that, your predictions get a whole lot more realistic—and you can skip the unnecessary panic. Instead, you’ll start to notice the deeper forces that really drive change—and maybe even spot opportunities that others miss.
